title: Detection of Unauthorized Network Firewall Rule Modification
shortTitle: Detection of Unauthorized Network Firewall Rule Modification
summary: This detection strategy covers unauthorised modification of network firewall rules, mapped to T1686.002, where an adversary disables, weakens or adds firewall policy on a host or network device to allow traffic that policy previously blocked. It matters because firewall rules are the primary control that keeps command and control, remote access and lateral movement channels closed, and an attacker who can edit them can open a path that looks legitimate to everything upstream. Detection relies on the firewall rule change audit records themselves, which name the rule, the direction and the acting process, the process creation events for the tools used to change policy, and the connection records that appear from a host immediately after a rule is loosened. Its main practical weakness is that firewall management is a normal administrative task performed by several tools and automation platforms, so the rule has to separate approved change pipelines from interactive edits, and it is blind wherever host firewall change auditing is not enabled or where the edit is made through a management console that does not log the acting process.

beginner.definition: A firewall is a list of rules that decide which network traffic is allowed in and out. This rule looks for changes to those rules. It cares most about changes that allow traffic which was blocked before. Such a change can quietly open a door for an attacker.
beginner.whyItMatters: Firewall rules are one of the main barriers in a network. An attacker who turns off a rule or adds a permissive one can keep control of a machine. The change itself is usually logged, which is lucky. The attacker is otherwise invisible.
howItWorks: The operating system can record every change to a firewall rule, including additions, deletions and edits.
The record names the rule and says whether it applies to incoming or outgoing traffic.
The rule also uses process creation records. That shows which tool and which account made the change.
It compares the change with the list of approved management tools, accounts and change windows.
It flags changes that allow broad traffic, disable a rule, or open a common remote access port.
It then checks network connection records from that host to see if traffic immediately started using the new rule.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman with a list of doors that must stay locked. Someone edits the list to say the side door may stay open. The watchman walks past it and thinks all is well. A second watchman who checks the list itself would notice the new line.
takeaways: Firewall rule changes are logged, so they are one of the few attacker actions you can see directly.
The strongest signals are a disabled rule and a new allow rule for remote access.
You need a list of approved management tools and accounts before this rule can be useful.

objectives: Explain how firewall rules control traffic and why attackers modify them.
Identify the firewall rule change audit records and the fields that name the rule, action and acting process.
Distinguish approved management tooling and automation from interactive rule edits.
Recognise high risk changes such as disabling rules or allowing inbound remote access ports.
Correlate a rule change with the outbound or inbound connections that follow it on the same host.
Evaluate which hosts and network devices in your environment have change auditing enabled.
dataSources: Windows Security firewall rule change audit records that report a rule being added, modified or deleted, including the rule name, direction and the process that requested the change
Windows Security event 4688 process creation and Sysmon event 1 process creation for firewall management utilities such as netsh and the PowerShell network security cmdlets
Sysmon event 3 network connection records from the host showing accepted connections to the newly permitted port after the change
Linux auditd and systemd records for changes to packet filter rulesets and firewall service reloads, including the acting user
Network device configuration change logs from perimeter and segment firewalls, with the managing account and the before and after rule content
logic: The pattern is a firewall policy change that is either made by a process or account outside the approved management set, or that results in a meaningful weakening of policy, such as disabling an existing rule, adding a broad allow rule, or permitting inbound traffic to a remote access port. The fields that must be correlated are the rule identity and direction, the action taken, the requesting process image and command line, the acting account, the host or device, and the timing relative to any approved change record. Adding the connection evidence afterwards is what turns a policy event into an intrusion indicator: a new inbound allow on a management port followed within minutes by a successful connection from an external address is very different from the same rule added days before any traffic appears. The benign case is configuration management or endpoint security software applying the approved baseline through a documented tool, and it normally produces a consistent rule set on many hosts in the same change window. The malicious case is an interactive tool, often a built-in command line utility, modifying a single host's rules outside a change window, frequently disabling logging or protection rules or opening remote access ports.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Host Firewall Rule Disabled or Broad Allow Added
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection_change:
#     EventType: 'firewall_rule_deleted'
#   selection_broad_allow:
#     EventType: 'firewall_rule_added'
#     Direction: 'Inbound'
#     RemoteAddress: 'Any'
#   selection_tool:
#     EventID: 1
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\\netsh.exe'
#       - '\\powershell.exe'
#   filter_mgmt:
#     User|endswith: '$'
#   condition: (selection_change or selection_broad_allow) and selection_tool and not filter_mgmt
# level: high
falsePositives: Endpoint security agents that add or refresh their own firewall rules during an agent upgrade
Software installers that create inbound allow rules for their own service on the local host
Configuration management pipelines that apply an approved firewall baseline to a group of servers
Administrators temporarily adding a diagnostic rule while troubleshooting a network issue, then removing it
Virtualisation platforms that adjust host firewall rules when a workload is migrated or resized
tuningNotes: Baseline the accounts and processes that legitimately edit firewall policy in your environment, then filter by that combination rather than by event type, so that the same account editing from a different tool still alerts. Add filters for application installer behaviour on user endpoints, since installers add local allow rules routinely, and scope the highest severity tier to servers, domain controllers and administrative hosts. Give extra weight to changes that delete or disable a rule, that allow any source address, or that open remote access ports, and require corroborating connection evidence before escalating to incident response. Keep an automated comparison of each host's firewall rule set against the approved baseline, which catches slow or disguised edits that a single event rule misses. Narrowing to approved tools loses coverage when an attacker uses a signed management tool with stolen credentials, so monitor those accounts for out of hours and off host edits.
